title: Tables, metatables, and modules
summary: Use a table as a map, resolve methods through __index, and review error handling that hides failures.

scenario.briefing: A game inventory module must track item counts and report bad data instead of masking it.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.
Review an artifact and identify the concrete risks.

hints: Inventory.__index = Inventory makes method lookup fall back to the module table.
setmetatable({ items = {} }, Inventory) attaches that fallback to each instance.
Read the current count with self.items[name] or 0 before adding.

misconceptions.description: Adding to a key that has never been set.
misconceptions.feedback: A missing key reads as nil, and arithmetic on nil raises an error. Default the read with or 0 before adding.

misconceptions.description: Using pcall to turn every error into a default value.
misconceptions.feedback: pcall returns false plus the error. Handle the failures you expect and let unexpected ones reach the caller.

sections.title: Tables are maps
sections.body: The same table type serves as a record, a map, and an array. Inventory keeps counts in items, keyed by the item name. Reading a key that has never been set returns nil, so the first insert must supply a default.

sections.title: Metatables route missing lookups
sections.body: setmetatable(stock, Inventory) gives stock a metatable. When a key is missing, Lua checks the metatable's __index. Setting Inventory.__index = Inventory makes the module table the fallback, so stock:add finds Inventory.add.

sections.title: Functions and modules
sections.body: A module is a table of functions and state. A colon definition such as function Inventory:add(name, count) receives self automatically, and callers use stock:add. A file module returns its table so require can load it once.

vocabulary.definition: Lua's compound value, usable as a sequence, map, or object.
A table that controls how another table handles missing keys and operators.
A table of functions and state that callers require or receive.

steps.title: Build an inventory module
steps.prompt: Edit main.lua. Inventory stores counts by name, resolves methods through __index, and totals the stock.

files.content:
local Inventory = {}
Inventory.__index = nil -- TODO: make Inventory the metatable's __index

function Inventory.new()
  return setmetatable({ items = {} }, Inventory)
end

function Inventory:add(name, count)
  self.items[name] = 0 -- TODO: add count to the current amount
end

function Inventory:total()
  local sum = 0
  for _, count in pairs(self.items) do
    sum = sum + count
  end
  return sum
end

local stock = Inventory.new()
stock:add("bolts", 3)
stock:add("nuts", 2)
print(stock:total())

tests.description: The module table keeps the taught name.
Instances fall back to the module through __index.
Adding to an unseen item starts from zero.

steps.title: Review the stock module
steps.prompt: Review the module and select every real problem.

artifact.title: stock.lua
artifact.caption: Missing keys and a broad pcall both turn failures into silent defaults.
artifact.content:
local function add_stock(stock, item, amount)
  stock[item] = stock[item] + amount
end

local function read_amount(source)
  local ok, amount = pcall(function()
    return source.amount + 0
  end)
  if not ok then
    return 0
  end
  return amount
end

findings.label: Adding amount to a missing key raises an arithmetic error on nil.
Using (stock[item] or 0) before the addition makes the first insert safe.
read_amount returns zero for every failure, so callers cannot distinguish bad data from a bug.
pcall makes read_amount safe because every error becomes a number.

verdicts.label: Block until missing keys and hidden errors are handled explicitly.

steps.explanation: A missing table key is nil, and nil + amount raises an error. Default it explicitly with (stock[item] or 0). read_amount also collapses every pcall failure into zero, so validate the field and report it, or let unexpected errors surface.
